title: Separating the variables
objectives: Solve a separable equation, including continuous compounding and logistic growth.

screens.title: A discount factor that shrinks
screens.prose: A discount factor $D(T)$ is today's value of £1 paid at $T$. Each extra year of waiting shrinks it at rate $r$: $\dfrac{dD}{dT} = -rD$, with $D(0) = 1$. Slide the rate and watch £100 paid in five years.
screens.question: Set $r$ to 4%. What is £100 in five years worth today?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the slider to 4% and read the marked point.

byKey.simple: You took off 4% of £100 for each of five years. Continuous discounting gives £81.87.
byKey.yearly: You discounted once a year, $100/1.04^5$. The equation discounts continuously.

explain.text: At 4% the point reads £81.87, which is $100e^{-0.2}$. The next screen shows where the exponential comes from.

screens.title: Separate, then integrate
screens.prose: The unknown $D$ appears on both sides, tangled with the rate. **Separating the variables** moves every $D$ to the left and every $T$ to the right. Then each side can be integrated on its own.
screens.question: Take the equation to its solution, one step at a time.

ops.label: Integrate both sides as they stand
ops.why: The right side holds $D$, an unknown function of $T$. Gather every $D$ on the left first.

ops.label: Exponentiate, then add $C$
ops.why: $e^{-rT + C} = e^{C}e^{-rT}$: the constant multiplies, it does not add.

hints.text: Get $D$ and $dD$ together on one side.

feedback.correct: $D = e^{-rT}$: separate, integrate, exponentiate, fit the start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move every $D$ to one side before you integrate.

explain.text: Dividing by $D$ (it is never 0 here) separates the variables. One constant from integrating becomes the factor $A = e^C$, and $D(0) = 1$ sets $A = 1$.

screens.title: A rate that changes with time
screens.prose: Now the rate rises: $r(t) = 0.03 + 0.01t$, so $B' = (0.03 + 0.01t)B$. It still separates: $\int dB/B = \int (0.03 + 0.01t)\,dt$, giving $B = B_0e^{0.03t + 0.005t^2}$.
screens.question: £1,000 grows under this rate. What is it after two years, to the penny?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $t = 2$ into the exponent $0.03t + 0.005t^2$.

byKey.flat: You kept the rate at 3%. It rises, so the exponent gains $0.005t^2$.
byKey.end: You charged the year-two rate, 5%, for both years. The exponent is the integral of the rate.

explain.text: The exponent is $\int_0^2 r(s)\,ds = 0.06 + 0.02 = 0.08$, so $B(2) = £1{,}083.29$. In general a discount factor is $e^{-\int r}$.

screens.title: The logistic by partial fractions
screens.prose: Growth that saturates: $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{K}\right)$. It separates, but the left side needs partial fractions: $\dfrac{1}{P(1 - P/K)} = \dfrac{1}{P} + \dfrac{1}{K - P}$. One tempting line is wrong; leave it out.
screens.question: Put the solution in order.

lines.text: $\dfrac{dP}{P(1 - P/K)} = k\,dt$, dividing where $P \ne 0$ and $P \ne K$
$\ln P - \ln(K - P) = kt + C$, integrating for $0 < P < K$
$\dfrac{P}{K - P} = Ae^{kt}$ with $A = \dfrac{P_0}{K - P_0}$, exponentiating and setting $t = 0$
$\ln P + \ln(K - P) = kt + C$, integrating term by term
lines.why: The integral of $\dfrac{1}{K - P}$ is $-\ln(K - P)$: the inner derivative is $-1$.

hints.text: Which step must come before you can integrate?
Partial fractions turn one fraction into two easy integrals.
Order: separate, partial fractions, integrate, exponentiate, solve for $P$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate first, then split the fraction, then integrate.

byKey.x: You integrated $\dfrac{1}{K - P}$ to $+\ln(K - P)$. The inner derivative is $-1$, so it is $-\ln(K - P)$.

explain.text: Each line follows from the one before by the reason written beside it. The minus sign in line 3 comes from the chain rule on $K - P$.

screens.title: A broker's client base
screens.prose: A broker has $P_0 = 1{,}000$ clients, room for $K = 10{,}000$ and growth rate $k = 0.8$ a year. So $P = \dfrac{10000}{1 + 9e^{-0.8t}}$. Slide $k$ to see the S-shape stretch and squeeze.
screens.question: With $k = 0.8$, how many clients are there after three years?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $t = 3$ into $10000/(1 + 9e^{-0.8t})$ with $k = 0.8$.

byKey.exp: You grew $1000e^{0.8t}$ with no ceiling. That passes $K$ before year 3.
byKey.lin: You multiplied 1,000 by $0.8 \times 3$. The growth is exponential at first, not linear.

explain.text: $e^{-2.4} = 0.0907$, so $P(3) = 10000/1.8165 = 5{,}505.21$. Growth is fastest at $K/2$ and dies away near $K$.

screens.title: A solution that blows up
screens.prose: Take $y' = y^2$ with $y(0) = 1$. Separating gives $-1/y = t + C$, so $C = -1$ and $y = \dfrac{1}{1 - t}$. The rate grows with the value, faster than any exponential.
screens.question: What is $y(0.5)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $t = 0.5$ into $1/(1 - t)$.

byKey.lin: You stepped once with the starting slope, $1 + 0.5$. The slope grows as $y$ does.
byKey.exp: You solved $y' = y$. With $y^2$ the growth is faster: $1/(1 - t)$.

explain.text: $y(0.5) = 2$, and as $t \to 1$ the value runs to infinity. The solution has no value at $t = 1$: it exists only on $t < 1$.

screens.title: Where the constant goes
screens.prose: For $y' = 0.5y$ with $y(0) = 3$, a colleague writes $\ln|y| = 0.5t + C$, then $y = e^{0.5t} + C$, so $C = 2$. The chart shows his curve. Drag the point and compare the slope with $0.5y$.
screens.question: Which is the general solution of $y' = 0.5y$?

options.why: You added the constant after exponentiating. $e^{0.5t + C} = e^Ce^{0.5t}$, so it multiplies.
You stopped at $\ln|y|$. Exponentiate to get $y$ itself.
Two constants for a first-order equation is one too many, and the $+C$ fails the equation.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Exponentiate $\ln|y| = 0.5t + C$ carefully.

byKey.add: You added the constant after exponentiating. The slope of $e^{0.5t} + 2$ is $0.5e^{0.5t}$, short of $0.5y$ by 1.

explain.text: $e^{0.5t + C} = e^C \cdot e^{0.5t}$, a multiple of $e^{0.5t}$. The added 2 leaves the slope at $0.5e^{0.5t}$, which is $0.5y - 1$, so the equation fails everywhere.

screens.title: The method, and what it can lose
screens.prose:
For $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = g(t)h(y)$, divide by $h(y)$ and integrate each side:

$$\int \frac{dy}{h(y)} = \int g(t)\,dt + C.$$

Dividing is allowed only where $h(y) \ne 0$. Every root $y^*$ of $h$ gives a constant solution $y = y^*$, which the formula can miss.
screens.question: Select all that apply: which constant functions solve the logistic $P' = kP(1 - P/K)$?

options.why: You took the point of fastest growth. There $P' = kK/4$, not 0.
The starting value is a constant only if it is already 0 or $K$.

feedback.correct: $P = 0$ and $P = K$: there the right side is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A constant works where the right side is 0.

explain.text: $h(P) = P(1 - P/K)$ is zero at $P = 0$ and $P = K$, so both are constant solutions. The formula gives $P = K$ when $P_0 = K$, but $P = 0$ never: we put it back by hand.

screens.title: The logistic in NumPy
screens.prose: Code the solution from the derivation, vectorised over `t`. Then invert it: from $\dfrac{P}{K - P} = \dfrac{P_0}{K - P_0}e^{kt}$ with $P = fK$, the time to reach a fraction $f$ is $\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\dfrac{f(K - P_0)}{(1 - f)P_0}$.

hints.text: `np.exp` works on arrays, so the formula vectorises as written.
The time is `np.log(frac * (K - p0) / ((1 - frac) * p0)) / k`.
Raise first: `if not (p0 / K <= frac < 1): raise ValueError(...)`.

feedback.correct: The closed form and its inverse, with a guard for fractions the curve never reaches.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the formula and raise `ValueError` when `frac` is below $P_0/K$ or at least 1.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with a return statement.

explain.text:
The guard matters: the curve starts at $P_0/K$ and only approaches 1.

```python
if not (p0 / K <= frac < 1):
    raise ValueError("frac must lie between p0/K and 1")
```

screens.title: Fitting growth too early
screens.prose: A fund's assets start at £1,000m and grow as the broker's clients did: $k = 0.8$, capacity £10,000m. An analyst fits $1000e^{0.8t}$ to the first few months, where the two curves agree.
screens.question: What does the exponential fit predict for year 3, in £m?

hints.text: Ignore the ceiling: that is the analyst's mistake.

feedback.correct: $1000e^{2.4} \approx £11{,}023$m, twice the logistic's £5,505m and past capacity.

byKey.log: That is the logistic's value. The question asks what the exponential fit predicts.

explain.text: Early on $P \approx P_0e^{kt}$ because $1 - P/K \approx 1$. By year 3 the fit says 11,023.18 (£m), above the £10,000m ceiling. Fitting a pure exponential to early adoption overshoots.

ideas: When $y' = g(t)h(y)$, move every $y$ to one side and integrate each side once, with one constant.
The constant of integration becomes a factor after exponentiating: $y = Ae^{kt}$, never $e^{kt} + C$.
Dividing by $h(y)$ loses the constant solutions at its roots; put them back by hand.

formula.name: Separation of variables
formula.note: A discount factor is $e^{-\int r}$; the logistic is $K/(1 + \frac{K - P_0}{P_0}e^{-kt})$.

summary.trap: Adding the constant after exponentiating: $\ln|y| = kt + C$ gives $Ae^{kt}$.

quiz.question: When do they reach half of $K$, in years, to 4 decimal places?

byKey.half: You solved $e^{0.8t} = 2$, a doubling time. Half of $K$ needs $e^{0.8t} = 9$.
byKey.k: You took $\ln 9$ and forgot to divide by $k = 0.8$.

options.why: $ty^2 = t \cdot y^2$, a product of a function of $t$ and one of $y$.

feedback.correct: $t + y$ is a sum, not a product, so it cannot be split.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the right side that is not a product $g(t)h(y)$.

explain.text: $y' = t + y$ is linear but not separable: no rearrangement puts every $y$ on one side. Lesson 3 solves it with an integrating factor.

quiz.question: What is the discount factor for two years, to 4 places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the rate, then take $e^{-\int r}$.

byKey.flat: You discounted at 3% for both years, $e^{-0.06}$.
byKey.pos: You grew instead of discounting. The factor is below 1.

explain.text: $\int_0^2 (0.03 + 0.01t)\,dt = 0.08$, so $D = e^{-0.08} = 0.9231$. It is the reciprocal of the growth factor 1.0833.

quiz.question: At what time does the solution blow up?

feedback.correct: $-1/y = t - 1/2$ gives $y = 2/(1 - 2t)$, which blows up at $t = 0.5$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate: $-1/y = t + C$, then use $y(0) = 2$.

byKey.one: You reused $y(0) = 1$. A larger start blows up sooner.
byKey.two: You took the starting value as the time.

explain.text: $C = -1/2$, so $y = 1/(1/2 - t) = 2/(1 - 2t)$, which has no value at $t = 0.5$.
